Good afternoon, Chair Cabán. Good afternoon, staff and forthcoming members of the Committee. I’m Doctor Alister Martin, Commissioner of Health at the New York Department of

Health and Mental Hygiene. I’m joined today by our Chief Financial Officer Aaron Anderson, Executive Deputy Commissioner Dr. Jean Wright, Assistant Commissioner Dr. Rebecca Linn-Walton, and Assistant Commissioner Jamie Neckles. Thank you for the– it is. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today on our Preliminary Budget as it relates to mental health. This is my first time testifying before the Committee on Mental Health and Substance Use, and so I would like to briefly introduce myself. I found public health by working in the emergency department. It soon became clear to me that many of my patients were in the ER not because of an acute health emergency, but because every other system had failed them. The ER was the last place for them to turn. I learned how much upstream systems matter by watching them fail again and again. There’s one particular story in particular I’d like to share with you. On the sixth day of my emergency medicine training as an intern, a woman came into the ER at 2:30 a.m. She was wheeling a suitcase behind her. My patient sat before me with smudged mascara, shoulders curved inward, and hands knotted in the sleeves of her sweatshirt. She

told me her story. After surgery to fix a shattered ankle, she came home with a row of neat white pills for the pain. When her oxy prescription ran out, she turned to her husband’s old bottles in the bathroom cabinet. When that, too, ran dry, she found herself accepting pills through a half-opened car window behind a CVS. The night she came into the ER, she showed up because she wanted her life back. She asked me for help, and I naively thought that I could help her. But when I asked my attending, the supervising doctor, about next steps, he told me something simple, discharge her. There was nothing we could do to help: in his words, it was “just not what we do here.” I did what I was told. I sent her away. I would like to think she got the help she needed, but the truth is I don’t know what happened to that woman. What I knew was that I didn’t want that to happen again to her, or to anyone else. Driven by that experience with my patient, I founded Get Waivered to help ER clinicians obtain the waivers they need to treat substance use disorder on the spot. The program grew into a national movement, helping thousands of providers re-envision the

emergency department as a front door for addiction treatment. Above all else, this patient showed me that there are so many larger systems we need to invest in to change the circumstances that bring people to the ER in the first place. That is the kind of upstream work happening at the New York City Health Department, each and every day. Our mental health programming spans substance use, serious mental illness, support for justice-involved populations, youth mental health, supportive housing, and so much more. All of it is making a meaningful difference in the lives of New Yorkers every day. What I share with you today are just a few of the highlights. One of our most encouraging metrics of success is that in 2024, overdose deaths in New York City fell by 28 percent, and that’s the first decline that we’ve seen– significant decline that we’ve seen in nearly a decade. That did not happen by accident. It happened because of sustained public health investments and programs that meet New Yorkers where they are worked, without judgement and with resources that save lives. It happened because of community health workers like Ava and Miriam on our Response

and Engagement Teams. They walk the streets every single day and engage with New Yorkers one on one. I was out with them near Penn Station a few weekends ago, and Ava told me the story of a shift that she worked last summer. She and Miriam were working in the South Bronx when she came upon an unconscious man surrounded by bystanders. She administered Narcan, and she revived this man. She called EMS, and he made it to the hospital. Were it not for Ava, that man would not be here today. Again, that 28 percent decline is not passive. It is the result of years of deliberate investment in naloxone distribution, in harm reduction, and in programs like Relay. Relay is our hospital-based, peer-led overdose prevention program. Peer wellness advocates are sent into emergency departments to meet patients who wake up from a nonfatal overdose. As these patients recover, they are met with compassion, with connection, with care. Relay reached nearly 1,600 patients in 2025 alone; 95 percent of them accepted services in the ER. Relay is a monumental success. We recently expanded to Wyckoff Heights Medical Center in Brooklyn, which is now the 16th hospital that is

included in this program. Again, that 28 percent decline is not an accident and is not caused by any one program. It is only because of a broader network of harm reduction, resources, and community-based care. It is the result of the naloxone we help put into the hands of some 300,000 New Yorkers just last year. It is the result of Response and Engagement Team members like Ava and Miriam, who do the quiet, unsung work of representing this agency every single day, connecting New Yorkers to care, and sometimes reviving them in the field. It is also the result of coordinated engagement with you all at City Council, with community organizations, and with peers all rowing in the same direction. What we are seeing is an impact not just in the citywide data, but in alleviating the racial inequities too. For the first time since 2018, we saw overdose deaths decline among Black and Latino New Yorkers as well. That is what public health funding does. It saves lives. And the progress is continuing. Early 2025 data show the lowest quarterly death count since 2020. Of course, none of these challenges happen in a vacuum. For so many of our neighbors, medical issues are not the

underlying drivers of their mental health struggles and substance use disorders. It’s structural. Often, what New Yorkers need most is solid ground to stand on. They need a safe place to come home to. Everything else can follow from there. The most tangible way we can provide that is through supportive housing. We remain committed to the goal of the 15 over 15 program to develop 15,000 units of supportive housing, which provide affordable, independent, and permanent homes to New Yorkers who are unhoused and either have or are at risk of a serious mental illness or a substance use disorder. This year, we surpassed 13,000 units total of both 15/15 units and State-City partnership program units. We are well on our way to meeting or exceeding our goal. Especially in one of the most expensive cities in the world, these units are a lifeline for thousands of our neighbors. We also continue to invest in our crisis hotline: through 988, we provide confidential support services at all hours of the day and night, and 90 percent of calls are answered within 30 seconds, and we offer services in English and Spanish with interpretation services available in

over 200 languages. Our callers are trained to refer New Yorkers to the appropriate services and make sure that whatever their concerns are, they know they don’t have to face them alone. We want every person in our city to know that help is available. So earlier this week, we launched a social and digital 988 campaign in English, Spanish, and Chinese. That campaign is reaching New Yorkers right now and will continue through April. Now, I will turn to the funding that makes all of this work possible. At the New York City Health Department, mental hygiene care is critical to our overarching vision to achieve longer, healthier lives for all New Yorkers. Our Division of Mental Hygiene leads that work and employs about 600 people with an operating budget of $850 million for Fiscal Year 2027, as of the Preliminary Budget. We are grateful for that continued funding and are particularly encouraged to see a sustained city investment in our supportive housing portfolio and our Outreach and Syringe Litter teams. At the state level, we’re grateful for several investments in critical mental health programming, including $17.5 million to expand teen mental health

first aid for all tenth graders statewide. Finally, at the federal level, we are watching the administration’s actions very closely and have been gravely concerned to see national mental health infrastructure devalued over the last year. At the New York City Health Department, our federal funding is concentrated in our disease control and emergency preparedness divisions, and our Division of Mental Hygiene is not heavily reliant on federal funding, but every part of our agency is impacted by the rapidly changing public health landscape. Here in New York City, we will continue to meet mental health challenges of New Yorkers with compassion rather than criminalization, and I’m proud to lead an agency in a way that puts that into practice every single day. I am grateful for support at the state and city levels that allow us to do this life-saving work. Thank you for your attention, and we’re happy to take your questions. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Thank you. And we have also been joined by Council Member Narcisse on Zoom. She wanted to make sure that we knew.

Thank you.

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Okay. Great. I would like to start with the ACT and IMT teams and just a line of questioning there. So, we know the ACT teams, the treatment program for folks with serious mental illness who have high-service needs that are not being met in traditional settings. The ACT program provides essential team base high-intensity treatment and wraparound support services for individuals with SMI challenges, substance use disorders, frequent contact with the criminal legal system, experience with homelessness, etcetera, etcetera. What are the current Fiscal 2026 and Fiscal 2027 projected budgets for ACT, and how much of the current funding is contracted out?

Yeah, thank you for that question, and thank you for your leadership on this issue, Chair Cabán. You know, we see the ACT program as a critical part of our spectrum of services that we can provide for folks who are dealing with mental health crises, and so this is incredibly important tool in our tool kit, providing highly-specialized long-term care for New Yorkers who are struggling with mental health issues. I’m going

to hand it over to Aaron Anderson to talk a little bit about the budget to answer that question directly.
Sure. thanks for that question, Chair. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yeah, and if you could hit headcount also when you talk about the budget, too.
Sure. Sure. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yeah.
So, for ACT and FACT together, the FY 26 budget for the– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] Yeah.
current year is $27.8 million, and the FY 27 budget is $23.3 million. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Is there a reason why you lumped the amounts together for ACT and FACT? Can you separate it out?

Sure, I can get you the separate numbers for that, yeah.

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Okay.
But aside from that, so all of the teams are contracted out to– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] Okay.

mental health service providers, so there’s no headcount, department headcount. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: What I mean, even contracted headcount I guess is what I’m trying to say. Just because it helps us think about what the need is in relationship to the referral list and all those kinds of things.

I’ll just add here that an ACT team has a staffing pattern that’s established by state licensure. So it’s really– there’s excruciating detail on the New York State Office of Mental Health website. The staffing pattern ranges from about nine to 11 or 12 FTEs, with the FACT team having extra staffing to address the forensic issues. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: And ACT teams, in particular, they’re operating in all five boroughs?
Yeah. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Okay. What are the days and operation for those teams?
I’ll pass it to Assistant Commissioner Jamie Neckles.

They’re seeing clients typically, you know, during regular hours, but are expected to be available during other hours as needed. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Got it. And can you just list the providers that are contracted with for ACT teams?
Sure. I think we provided that in writing. I don’t have– I can pull it up. There’s about 20 or so different provider organizations. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Okay.

So, it’s a long list of–

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Great, thank you. So, that’s been submitted. Thank you. How many people are currently on the referral list for ACT, and then from that list, how are they prioritized?

Can I ask a follow– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] And I know– again, I know we talked about this at the last hearing that sometimes folks will qualify for ACT and IMT and, you know, figuring out those things. But curious how they are prioritized.
Are you asking about the waist list or the referral list, which– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] The wait list, yeah.
Okay, great. Well, first of all, we know that having a wait list is not the ideal scenario for what we’d like to– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] I know. I want you to have more money.

That’s right. And ultimately, folks who are on the waist list have the ability to be engaged by a care coordinator while they’re waiting, and so people have that right as

soon as they jump on that wait list. There’s a pretty large variation in terms of the numbers of the wait list. I’ll turn it over to Assistant Commissioner Jamie Neckles to talk a little bit about each one of those programs.

Thank you. We list our– it’s an important issue, so I’m glad you’re, you know, shining light on it. We’ve got 312 people on the waiting list and referral list– we use those terms interchangeably sometimes– at this point in time. And as the Commissioner said, everybody’s offered a care coordinator while waiting for a higher level of care. Some people are in other treatment programs while they’re waiting to be stepped up to an ACT team. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yeah. I mean, I’d be curious if there’s a breakdown on sort of like who’s engaged in programming while they’re waiting. What kinds of services people are getting. How many of those folks on a wait list maybe aren’t getting any services? And yeah, this is really important because in my mind the way I see it is, if there’s somebody on a wait list or referral list, their options then

become an emergency room or Rikers Island, and I think that’s what’s at stake. How long does an applicant wait in each stage of the process, from operation to approval, and then from approval to placement?
Hand it to Jamie to share more there.

Yeah. So, applications, too, are single point of access are submitted a treatment provider typically, most commonly as a part of a hospital. Discharge plan from community-based treatment providers on behalf of the person. The person themselves may not always fully realize that an application has been submitted on their behalf. I just want to point that out. And so they may or may not know that we– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] How do they find out? How do they find out when somebody else refers them? Is it just by the contact, or?
So, when we receive the application– CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: [interposing] Yeah.
and find a person eligible, we’ll connect them with an ACT team, and that ACT team goes out and finds the person. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Okay.
And sometimes that’s how the individual finds out. And sometimes that’s a surprise to them. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yeah.

The time at which they were referred, they may not have been– you know, they have been in a difficult position and not, you know, paying attention or fully, you know, absorbing or remembering everything that was going on. Totally understandable. So, the ACT teams are– it’s a difficult position, right, to show up at somebody’s door and you say hi, I know a lot about you. Would you– I’d like to, you know, help you. Sometimes that’s troubling to anybody, right, to have somebody knock on your door. So, it takes time for them to engage folks in care. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: But could you give a timeline?
Timeline? CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yeah.
So, yeah. So, the referrals are– that was your original question. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Yeah, sorry.

An application comes in– I got list in the human story. So, the application comes it, gets reviewed in a couple of business days. Depending on a number of factors, may influence the timeline to assignment to care. The most– the first priority goes to people who are mandated to mental health treatment through assisted outpatient treatment. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Okay.

So, we’re required by, you know, New York State law to prioritize access for those folks. And so they may get connected to a treatment team, you know, within a few days. Other folks may wait longer, may wait I think it’s up to about three months is the average

time from referral to enrollment in the program when that ACT team shows up at their door. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: And if you– so I understand you prioritize the mandated folks but for that other grouping of people. What does the prioritization look like? Sort of, what are the things that you’re looking for? I’m just going to throw out an example. Is it like, do you see if they have– they live with family, or like what are the things that you look at to figure out prioritization?

Sure. some of the things you mentioned earlier, you’re wondering about, you know, what’s going on with those folks on the referral list. Are they in treatment? So, if they’re in treatment, and it’s not optimal, but they’re somewhat connected, we would see that as less prioritized than somebody who’s not connected to any care without a mandate. So, it’ll be a factor like that, risk factors as well. If there’s, you know, more frequent hospitalizations, if we see a risk of harmful behavior towards self or others, that could also elevate the clinician’s decision.

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Thank you. And ACT is eligible for Medicaid.
Yes. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Do you have any concerns on the outlook in terms of Medicaid reimbursement and the– are you concerned about that right now?
I can– yeah. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: I just want it on the record. I mean, obviously, it’s an obvious answer, but we want it on the record.

Yeah, we are very concerned as an agency writ large. The federal administration’s posture towards health coverage for individuals who are– who have a history of being marginalized or disenfranchises is dangerous. It’s unfounded and something that, you know, we are fighting back on here in the [inaudible]. It certainly relates to the work that we do in mental hygiene, but it’s across the entire agency. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Totally. Can you talk briefly about specifically how ACT teams support the LGBTQIA+ community?

Yeah, I can start us off and then hand it over to Commissioner Neckles. You know, the ACT teams we provide individualized assessments and person-centered intervention for folks. And we really make sure that we meet the unique needs of each and every participant that comes onto our list, and that includes individuals in the LGBTQIA+ community. Let me hand it over to Assistant Commissioner Jamie Neckles to see if she has more to add.

I think that covered it well, right. The criteria are adults with serious mental illness, but everybody– all of us have sort of intersecting identities. And so certainly a person’s sexual orientation or gender identity may be one of those and that needs to be supported by the team in person-centered service planning.

And what I’ll say is we are 100 percent open to partnership and taking advice and guidance, you know, on this. So, looking forward to continuing those conversations.

CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Thank you. And I know that obviously the span of health care suport, mental health care support for specifically queer, trans, and gender-expansive communities is a hard environment, especially with private hospitals that they aren’t going to deliver care. And so yeah, I’m wondering– you know, we’ve talked a lot about, like, is H+H prepared to take on more clients? But I also wonder if there’s room for gaps to be filled in this way.
